winner.title: Amiwo With Grilled Chicken

evidence.authenticity: Toasts the corn flour, makes a slurry plus dry flour, and sets the amiwo in moulds, the same method as the UN Tourism/Georgiana Viou version. Uses vegetable oil rather than palm oil and adds dried shrimp powder and a Dijon mustard sauce. Brand-publisher post with little cultural context.
evidence.precision: Cup and spoon measures only, no weights. Every step has a time and most have a cue (onions soften, flour begins to brown, mixture thickens, liquid evaporated). Pan sizes not given. No chicken recipe.
evidence.testing: Some reasoning (toasting, two-stage flour addition, stirring so the bottom does not scorch), but no test kitchen and no explanation of why.
evidence.photos: One finished-dish photo plus a video I could not view. No process photos.
evidence.efficiency: Sauce is made while the amiwo sets. Steps are sensible and the times look realistic.
evidence.access: Shrimp powder is the only unusual item. Everything else is at a US grocery.

winner.why: It follows the traditional toast-and-mould technique and gives the most cues, while the other versions are thin or are crab variants.

runnerUp.title: Amiwo

evidence.authenticity: Corn porridge cooked in tomato and palm oil base, but it is a crab version, with no cultural context or named author.
evidence.precision: Cups and a few counts, with one weight (200 g crab). Cues: reduced and thick, pulls away from the pot sides. No pan size.
evidence.testing: No sign of testing or reasoning.
evidence.photos: No step images, 9 images on the page.
evidence.access: Crab meat is needed, but it offers crayfish as a substitute.

runnerUp.why: It has palm oil and a doneness cue, but it is a crab variant with less detail than the winner.

candidates.disqualified: Pâte rouge with beans, cumin and parsley and no palm oil, so it is a Westernized version rather than amiwo
